open-question.question: capture-milestone-principle-updates holds a temporary file path in a shell variable (SNAPSHOT="$(mktemp)") and uses it quoted, the one place runtime prose itself instructs a variable. Is the recorded invariant scoped so that this use stays allowed and untouched, or is the rule general enough that the snapshot idiom must be named as an exception or changed?
open-question.recommendation: The snapshot is one quoted value that word splitting never reaches, so the rule stays scoped to the goal's sites and one rationale sentence saying so stops a later editor from removing the idiom or citing it as a loophole; its reliance on shell state surviving between calls is a different failure that belongs in its own milestone, not in a rule widened to reach it.
open-question.alternative: The invariant covers only the two named sites, and its CLAUDE.md rationale says so explicitly. It names the capture snapshot as outside the rule because it is one quoted value, not a path list or a tool command. The capture skill's runtime prose stays unchanged. A later editor sees in the rationale's own wording why the snapshot stays, so it is neither "fixed" by mistake nor cited as a loophole. The runtime files and the goal's site list stay untouched. The rationale gains a sentence about a file the milestone otherwise leaves alone. Recording the snapshot as acceptable also signs off on the idiom while it still carries the cross-call fragility: on a host whose shell does not keep variables between calls, "$SNAPSHOT" is empty when step 7 restores or cleans up. Where that sentence sits is decided by the invariant-placement question.

The recorded invariant covers only the two sites the goal names: the paths in commit-procedure.md and the fixed open-question tool command at the multi-call sites. The capture-milestone-principle-updates snapshot idiom (SNAPSHOT="$(mktemp)", then "$SNAPSHOT" in the copy, restore, and cleanup commands) stays exactly as it is. Neither CLAUDE.md nor any runtime file mentions it. This is the smallest change and matches the goal's site list exactly. The snapshot is quoted and holds one value, so the word-splitting failure the milestone targets never reaches it, and no file outside the named sites is touched. Because the scope is never stated, a later editor who reads the rationale as a general "no variables" rule may "fix" the snapshot, or point to it as precedent for adding variables elsewhere. The idiom also keeps a separate fragility. The snapshot is set in step 6 and used in step 7 only after one or more conversation rounds, so on a host whose shell tool does not keep variables between calls, "$SNAPSHOT" expands to an empty string there: the restore cp fails and the cleanup silently leaks the temporary file.

The rationale states the rule by the failure it prevents, not by site. A value the shell has to split into several words (a path set, a multi-word command) is never held in a variable and is written out literally on every call. A single value used quoted is outside the rule. The snapshot complies without being named, and the capture skill stays unchanged. The reason carries over to any future site and explains on its own terms why the snapshot is fine, with no list of sites or exceptions to maintain. It is narrower than the goal's wording for the tool sites ("never through a variable, alias, or function"), which also bans aliases and functions that have nothing to do with splitting. So the rationale and the site prose would give different reasons, and the result depends on how the host-root wording question frames the ban next to the host-provided variable in the rendered command. It also says nothing about the snapshot's cross-call fragility.

The rationale states a general rule: runtime shell commands never hold a value in a variable the runner introduces itself. The capture snapshot is named in CLAUDE.md as the one deliberate exception, with the reason that it is a single quoted temporary path. Because runtime files carry no editor-facing prose, the capture skill's own text stays unchanged. The rule is broad enough to cover every site written in future, not only today's two, and the one deviation is listed where a later editor will look, so nothing is left implicit. The stated rule is broader than the goal's two sites, and the exception keeps a known weakness: where the shell does not keep variables between calls, "$SNAPSHOT" is empty when it is read in step 7. An exception list also invites more entries over time.

A general rule bans variables the runner introduces in every runtime shell command, with no exception. To comply, the capture skill is changed: step 6 runs mktemp alone, reads the path it prints, and copies the baseline to that path written literally. The step 7 cleanup and restore commands then use the same literal path, so the skill instructs no variable at all. One rule with no exception. It also removes the reliance on a variable surviving across separate shell calls and the review rounds between steps 6 and 7, so restore and cleanup work whatever the host's shell does with state. It goes beyond the goal's two named sites and rewrites a carefully worded restore step in a skill the goal does not mention. The runner must also carry an opaque generated path correctly over an unbounded number of conversation rounds, which swaps a shell-state risk for a transcription risk.

A general rule bans variables the runner introduces in every runtime shell command, with no exception. The capture skill drops mktemp and snapshots to one fixed, literally written path outside the working tree, used as written in the copy, restore, and cleanup commands. Nothing generated has to be remembered or transcribed across the review rounds, so restore and cleanup are the same literal commands in every run and do not depend on shell state. A fixed path collides between concurrent runs or two repositories, and a stale snapshot from an interrupted run could be restored over the store later. There is also no portable fixed location outside the repository that is not itself reached through a variable such as the temp-dir variable. On top of that it widens the milestone to a file the goal does not name.

The invariant stays scoped to the two named sites. Separately, as a robustness fix, the capture skill is changed to the literal mktemp path: run mktemp, read the printed path, and write it literally into the copy, restore, and cleanup commands. The rationale does not tie that change to the rule. It fixes the real cross-call weakness of the snapshot (an empty "$SNAPSHOT" at step 7 where shell state does not persist) without making the recorded rule broader than the failure the milestone targets. It adds work outside the goal's stated scope with no rule to motivate it. A later reader sees a variable-free snapshot next to a site-scoped rule and may infer a general ban that was never recorded. As with the other literal-path option, the runner has to carry the generated path across conversation rounds.

open-question.question: The Claude host renders the {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder as the host-provided reference ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, so the fixed open-question tool command as shipped there already contains one variable. How should the "never through a variable" rule be worded so that it bans variables the runner introduces itself without contradicting the command it sits beside, given that core/ files may name no host?
open-question.recommendation: Banning only a variable, alias, or function the runner defines itself keeps all three mechanisms the goal names, leaves the host-provided reference outside the ban without singling it out, reads the same in every rendered tree, and is short enough to sit as one clause; the unqualified wording leaves a contradiction on the page, the copy-as-shown wording drops the ban the goal asks for, and a per-host slot is a build change the goal excludes.
open-question.alternative: The rule keeps the goal's prohibition vocabulary and limits it to things the runner introduces itself. It is worded along the lines of "write the full command shown on every call; never define a variable, alias, or function of your own to stand for it or any part of it." The command it sits beside stays untouched. The sentence does not mention the plugin-root segment, and core/ prose names no host and no shell. It is the smallest change that still names variable, alias, and function, the three mechanisms the goal bans. Because the ban covers only what the runner defines, the host-provided reference in the Claude render is left out without being singled out. The wording reads the same in both rendered trees. The exemption is only implied. A runner reading the Claude render still sees "never … a variable" next to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} and has to infer from "of your own" that the reference is allowed. Whether this one sentence fits depends on where the sibling Tool-site rule placement question puts the rule: in each file's contract sentence, or repeated at every fenced call.

The rule bans variables, aliases, and functions the runner introduces, and it also says outright that the plugin-root part of the command is written exactly as shown. That part is described by its role, not by any host's spelling. Example wording: "the plugin-root path at the head of the command is part of the fixed command and is written as shown." The rendered command stays unchanged, and core/ still names no host. It removes the apparent contradiction on the page rather than leaving it to inference. A runner looking at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is told directly that the reference belongs to the command and is not the kind of variable the rule bans. The sentence gets longer at every site that carries it. The Antigravity render, where the plugin root is the plain literal .agents/plugins/cairn, gets a clause about a reference that isn't there as a variable. That cuts against the CLAUDE.md rule of at most one sentence of tool contract per site. How heavy this is depends on the sibling Tool-site rule placement question.

The rule is worded only as a positive instruction to reproduce the command exactly as shown on every call, never abbreviated or rebuilt. Example: "write the command exactly as shown, in full, on every call." The words variable, alias, and function do not appear, so nothing can contradict the variable reference in the Claude render. The command and the host rendering stay unchanged. It can't contradict any host's render, because it doesn't use the vocabulary that clashes and it treats whatever the command contains as part of the fixed text. It is also the shortest wording, and it reads the same in every host tree. It drops the explicit "never through a variable, alias, or function" that the goal's text calls for, so the milestone's stated rule is only implied. A runner may not see that storing the command prefix in a shell variable and expanding it unquoted counts as not writing it out in full. That idiom is exactly the word-splitting failure this milestone targets.

The build gains a new per-host slot in scripts/hosts/<host>/settings.toml, filled into the rule sentence the same way {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} is filled now. Each host tree then gets wording fitted to its own command: the Claude host's sentence can name its plugin-root variable as the one allowed reference, and the Antigravity sentence needs no exemption at all. The core/ source carries only the placeholder and names no host. Each rendered tree reads precisely for the command it actually ships, with no inference and no clause about a reference that isn't there. The core/ rule against naming a host is kept, because the host-specific text lives in the declarative host definitions. It changes the build and its validation, which the goal doesn't ask for: a new slot constant, a fill step, unfilled-slot coverage, and a filled value in every host definition, all for one sentence of prose. It is a step toward the kind of structural fix the goal puts out of scope. It also adds a second per-host prose value that has to be kept in sync by hand.

The rule goes into runtime prose exactly as the goal words it: "write the full fixed command on every call, never through a variable, alias, or function". It has no origin scoping and no mention of the plugin-root segment. The host-provided reference is left for the runner to read as part of the fixed command. Any account of the tension goes only into the CLAUDE.md rationale, which runners in user projects never see. It adds nothing to the runtime prose beyond what the goal already specifies, so every site gets the shortest and most literal form of the stated rule. In practice the fixed command is shown right beside the rule, so the reference is plainly part of what is to be written out. On the Claude host the rule says "never through a variable" next to a command that contains one. That is the contradiction the question raises, left for each runner to resolve on its own. A literal-minded runner might try to expand or avoid ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, which it cannot do correctly because only the host resolves that path.

open-question.question: The answer sweep's per-question lift call lives in core/shared/answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md, which the goal does not list among the multi-call tool sites although the sweep runs it once per question. Does that procedure get the full-command rule too, or is the rule stated only in the five files the goal names?
open-question.recommendation: The lift repeats only inside the sweep, and the sweep's own sentence is read before the first call of the run, so wording it to cover the calls of the procedures it follows guards the lift where it actually repeats without editing a file outside the goal's list or adding rule text for the single-question skill that makes the call once.
open-question.alternative: answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md is left unchanged. Instead, the rule the answer sweep's SKILL.md states is worded explicitly to cover every tool call the run makes. That includes the per-question calls of the procedures it follows: the lift procedure's lift, and answer-procedure.md's locate, remove, and cascade remove. The edit stays within the five named files, and the coverage reaches the lift call only where it is actually repeated. It covers the lift exactly where it repeats (the sweep loop) without editing a file outside the goal's list. It also adds no rule text to a procedure whose other runner, the single-question skill, makes the call only once. The rule is stated in the sweep's SKILL.md, away from the fenced lift command it governs, so a runner following the procedure file sees no rule at the call itself. Whether that works depends on how the "Tool-site rule placement" sibling settles. A rule repeated at every fenced call has no fenced lift call in the sweep's own file to attach to.

The rule is stated only in the five files the goal names: review-milestone-requirements, the two annotating passes, the answer sweep's SKILL.md, and answer-procedure.md. core/shared/answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md is left unchanged. The answer sweep's own rule is worded to cover the calls that file shows, and nothing more. The lift call keeps its fenced full command with no rule beside it. It matches the goal's explicit list and its "two provoking sites" framing, so the milestone's scope and diff stay as small as defined. The lift call already appears as the full fixed command in its own fenced block, so a runner copying it verbatim never needs a variable. The sweep runs the lift once per question, so it is one of the most repeated calls in any run. A runner factoring that repeated command into a variable or function is exactly the failure the milestone targets. Leaving it uncovered leaves a known multi-call path unguarded while answer-procedure.md, which the same sweep loop runs, is covered.

alternative.id: Add lift procedure as sixth site

open-question.alternative: answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md gets the same rule as the five named sites. It becomes a sixth rule site, stated in that file beside its one lift call. The rule then reaches both runners that follow the procedure: the answer sweep, once per question, and answer-open-question-with-recommendation, once per run. recommend-procedure.md and the single-call sites stay as they are. The rule sits next to the call it governs, in the file the runner actually reads when it makes that call. Every tool call the sweep's per-question loop makes is then covered: the lift here, and the locate, remove, and cascade in answer-procedure.md. No site depends on the sweep's SKILL.md text carrying over into a procedure it delegates to. It goes beyond the goal's literal list of five. Unlike the named sites, this file has no tool-contract sentence today, so the rule needs a new sentence there instead of an addition to an existing one. How well that fits depends on how the "Tool-site rule placement" sibling settles where the rule sits in a file. The single-question skill that also follows this procedure makes only one lift call, so for that runner the rule guards a repetition that does not happen.

The rule is stated in every runtime file under core/ that carries the open-question tool command, not only in the multi-call sites. That is about thirteen files, including answer-with-recommendation-procedure.md, recommend-procedure.md, answer-open-question-with-alternative, discuss-open-question, modify-milestone-goal, derive-tasks, ask-in-milestone-context, and the alternatives agent. The full-command rule then becomes uniform wherever the command appears, with no multi-call test deciding which sites get it. It needs no judgment about which sites count as multi-call, so a site that later starts calling the tool repeatedly is already covered. It also matches the existing invariant that the invocation is "the one fixed command" at every site. It widens the milestone well past the goal's "two provoking sites" and its explicit list of five, touching around thirteen files. Most of those are single-call sites where nothing tempts a variable, so most of the added prose guards nothing. It also expands the hosts/ rebuild diff and goes against the goal's deliberately narrow scope.
